headline: AI system 'Star Fleet' solves 20 Erdős Problems using 20 parallel GPT-5.6 instances
summary: Star Fleet, a Mac desktop app, leverages 20 custom agentic 'starships' each running a GPT-5.6 instance on a dedicated 60-vCPU server to tackle complex mathematical challenges.
details: Star Fleet is an AI system designed to solve the world's hardest open mathematics problems, implemented as a Mac desktop application. It operates by controlling up to 20 custom agentic 'starships' in parallel.

Each 'starship' runs its own GPT-5.6 instance on a dedicated 60-vCPU server, allowing the system to work on multiple separate math problems simultaneously. The entire system is built from scratch using TypeScript and Bun.

The developers made a significant effort to avoid problems with informal or partial answers already available online, focusing strictly on genuinely open mathematical challenges. This ensures the integrity of the solutions found.

One notable success includes Erdős Problem #123, a number theory problem with a $250 prize, which asks if every large integer is a sum of distinct terms of a specific form, none of which divide any other. Star Fleet successfully proved the theorem Erdos123.erdos_123.

The core difficulty of such problems often lies in the divisibility condition, which makes ordinary completeness arguments challenging. A set chosen to be a divisibility antichain can be too sparse to fill consecutive integers.

Earlier work provided a reduction scheme, but it left a 'stubborn finite-seed problem' requiring representation of integers within a specific interval. This limitation prevented several partial ideas from fully solving the problem.

Star Fleet's approach involves a structural simplification: working on one homogeneous exponent level. This turns the problem into an additive question about subset sums, making primitiveness essentially free.

The system employs an edge-code construction to supply primitive subset sums with distinct residues and a bounded carry. This, combined with finite van der Waerden's theorem, generates long exact arithmetic progressions of primitive homogeneous subset sums.

Further techniques include a bounded homogeneous-radix lemma, which proves coefficient sums contain a full interval of significant width. This is then realized as an interval on a lattice of a specific step.

Finally, a primitive correction for each residue modulo any prescribed modulus is constructed on sufficiently high exact degrees. These corrections are supported on coordinate faces and are disjoint from the strict-interior AP terms, allowing residue gluing to convert the lattice interval into a complete solution.
